<reflection>
- The first experiment (S=2.0, cat=0.05, P=0.0) resulted in very similar NLL values for most models (around -23.7 to -23.9), with only M5 being strongly ruled out and M3/M4 showing slightly worse fits.
- This indicates that under standard conditions, the additional parameters in the more complex models can be tuned to mimic the simple Michaelis-Menten mechanism (M1). My aim to broadly separate the mechanisms was only partially achieved, as the baseline condition did not trigger the distinguishing features of most models.
- To force the models to diverge, we need to perturb the system using the other available experimental levers: initial product concentration and a significantly different catalyst concentration.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
I propose an experiment with a high initial product concentration (P=0.5) and a high initial catalyst concentration (cat=0.20), while keeping the substrate at a moderate level (S=1.0). 
1. The high initial product concentration will immediately trigger product-induced deactivation mechanisms (M12, M17). If these mechanisms are true, the reaction will show an unusually slow initial rate or rapid plateau compared to models without product effects.
2. The high catalyst concentration (4x higher than the first experiment) will amplify any second-order catalyst interactions, such as dimerization (M2, M3) or bimolecular catalyst deactivation (M13, M18, M19). These models will scale non-linearly with the increased catalyst concentration, distinguishing them from first-order catalyst models.
3. By combining these two perturbations, we prevent the models from simply rescaling their rate constants to fit the data, as the kinetic dependencies on [P] and [cat] are fundamentally different across the candidate mechanisms.
</hypothesis>
